query: Which method can be used for the presence of ferromagnetic ground states, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Spin‐polarized magnetometry measurements (e.g. via SQUID or VSM) can be used to verify the presence of a ferromagnetic ground state in alloys that contain ferromagnetic elements (such as Co) by detecting spontaneous remanent magnetization and low coercivity at low temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized high-entropy alloy (HEA) containing a significant fraction of ferromagnetic elements (e.g., AlCoFeNi) exhibiting a B2 or related ordered phase.
generation.intervention: Subject the sample to magnetic characterization using SQUID or high-sensitivity vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) at cryogenic temperatures (e.g. below 100 K) following a proper heat treatment to minimize compositional segregation.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under zero-field-cooled (ZFC) and field-cooled (FC) conditions over a temperature range (e.g. 10 K – 300 K) with applied magnetic fields sufficiently low to capture the spontaneous magnetization behavior.
generation.structural_mediator: Ferromagnetic domains resulting from clustering of Co-rich regions or ordered magnetic phases within the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: In a ferromagnetic ground state, exchange interactions promote parallel alignment of magnetic moments; these should yield a hysteresis loop with non-zero remanence and low coercivity at low temperatures. The spin polarization inherent in the material would manifest as a measurable spontaneous magnetization even in the absence of an external field.
generation.predicted_outcome: SQUID or VSM measurements will reveal a clear hysteresis loop with a finite saturation magnetization, remanent magnetization, and low coercivity at low temperatures, confirming the ferromagnetic ground state.
generation.baseline: A similar alloy processed identically but with substitution of the ferromagnetic element (e.g. partial replacement of Co with Cr which is antiferromagnetic) is expected to show a significantly reduced or absent ferromagnetic signature.
generation.boundary: The method is effective so long as the sample has sufficiently low competing magnetic phases (e.g. antiferromagnetic or paramagnetic constituents) and the magnetic signal is not masked by extrinsic effects such as compositional inhomogeneity or measurement noise.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative values such as the exact saturation magnetization and coercivity may depend on sample processing details, grain size, and elemental partitioning; therefore, while the method is qualitatively reliable, precise numerical comparisons require careful calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set with a high concentration of ferromagnetic elements (e.g., standard AlCoFeNi alloy) and another set where a substantial portion of the ferromagnetic element is substituted with an antiferromagnetic one (e.g., replacing 50% of Co with Cr). Subject both sets to identical low-temperature SQUID magnetometry measurements (ZFC/FC protocols) and compare the magnetic hysteresis loops.
measurements: Temperature dependence of magnetization (M vs. T curves)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ferromagnetic sample does not show a well-defined hysteresis loop with significant remanence and low coercivity at low temperatures, or if the magnetic response of the Co-rich sample is not substantially different from the Cr-substituted sample, then the method would be considered ineffective in detecting a ferromagnetic ground state.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, combined with annealing temperature, influence the hierarchical phase decomposition, microhardness, and magnetic properties in AlCoFeNi-based high entropy alloys?. System: AlCoFeNi and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi (near-equiatomic HEAs). Processing: Arc melting of elemental pellets (99.9% purity) under argon atmosphere, followed by isothermal annealing at 600 °C and 1000 °C for 15 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Annealing at 600 °C/15 h and 1000 °C/15 h; characterization via SEM, TEM, APT, EBSD, Vickers microhardness, and magnetic measurements (Ms, Hc). Findings: AlCoFeNi annealed at 1000 °C forms a single ordered B2 phase with a microhardness of 406 VHN, saturation magnetization (Ms) of 111.6 emu/g, and coercivity (Hc) of 4.3 Oe.; AlCoFeNi annealed at 600 °C decomposes into a B2 matrix and fine Fe-Co rich BCC precipitates, increasing microhardness to 474 VHN and Hc to 14.5 Oe while reducing Ms to 99.8 emu/g.; Substituting 50% Co with Cr in AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi induces phase separation into B2 + BCC even at 1000 °C, with Ms dropping to 42.2 emu/g and Hc rising to 39.4 Oe.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi anneal
